newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. envoy says Serb hardliners are main problem.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy says Serb hardliners are main problem.

text.p: U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke travelled to the Bosnian capital on Thursday to lean on ultra-nationalist Serb leaders blamed for undermining the peace accords he helped broker in 1995.

The American diplomat who engineered the Dayton peace agreement returned to the Balkans this week to bring pressure to bear on the leaders of Bosnia, Croatia and Yugoslavia in a bid to speed up the stalled peace process.
Holbrooke planned to meet the multi-ethnic central cabinet and members of Bosnia's collective presidency, including Serb hardliner Momcilo Krajisnik.

He said on Wednesday that it was Krajisnik and other allies of indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic who were primarily to blame for blocking enforcement of the peace treaty which ended four years of war in former Yugoslavia.
"The major problem is all-out obstruction by leaders in Pale," Holbrooke told reporters, referring to Karadzic's headquarters outside Sarajevo.
Holbrooke met Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and the Moslem chairman of Bosnia's presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, on Wednesday in the Adriatric port of Split.

The two presidents condemned recent violence against refugees and pledged to protect Bosnians trying to return to their pre-war homes. They also agreed to set up proper border posts and promote economic cooperation between the two countries.
It was Holbrooke's first visit to the region since he negotiated a deal last year that forced Karadzic to step down as Bosnian Serb president.
Under the agreement which was signed by Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic, Karadzic promised to stay out of politics.

One year later, Karadzic continues to wield power behind the scenes and his allies have sought to circumvent the Dayton accords which divided Bosnia into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories ruled by a small central government.
Serb hardliners loyal to Karadzic have blocked the return of Moslem and Croat refugees and tried to portray their autonomous territory as an independent state.
During his visit, Holbrooke planned to promote Karadzic's rival, Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who has been locked in a bitter power struggle with Karadzic.

Holbrooke, forced to change his schedule due to poor weather, was due to fly to the northwest town of Banja Luka on Friday to meet Plavsic before heading to neighbouring Yugoslavia for talks with President Slobodan Milosevic, the patron of the Bosnian Serbs.
Although an ultra-nationalist herself, Plavsic has won Western support in her battle with Karadzic, whom she has accused of running vast smuggling rackets.
Balkan analysts said Holbrooke would pledge U.S. backing for a general election which Plavsic called after dissolving parliament in Bosnia's Serb republic.
Political analysts said Holbrooke would push Milosevic to stop propping up Karadzic loyalists and threaten him with economic sanctions unless he abided by his Dayton commitments.

Before flying into Sarajevo, Holbrooke held talks with the chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, General John Shalikashvili, and NATO's top commander, General Wesley Clark, at an American base in the northeast town of Tuzla.
The fate of indicted war criminals, including Karadzic, who remain at large was expected to dominate Holbrooke's discussions.
Croatia and Yugoslavia have tried to avoid their obligations under the Dayton treaty to hand over fugitives wanted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal.
British soldiers in the NATO-led peace force arrested one suspect and shot dead another who opened fire last month in an unprecedented operation in the Serb-controlled Prijedor region.
The arrest operation set off a wave of retaliatory bombings against NATO and international monitors but the low-level violence has tapered off over the past week.
Some commentators speculated that Holbrooke might deliver an ultimatum, warning that NATO would go after more suspects if authorities failed to turn them over.
